content.title: About
content.content: Blackberry juice, 100% is a natural beverage obtained by pressing fresh blackberry berries without added sugar, preservatives or flavorings. It has a deep dark‑purple colour, a distinctive aroma and a mildly tart‑sweet taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Blackberries contain more than 20 different antioxidants, including anthocyanins that give the fruit its deep colour.
Blackberry juice is often used in culinary applications such as sauces, marinades and desserts.
In traditional Native American medicine, blackberries were used as a remedy for colds and inflammation.
If produced by cold‑press and quickly pasteurised, the juice retains a high proportion of vitamin C.
Blackberries grow in temperate climates and are harvested in late summer to early autumn.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Antioxidants help neutralise free radicals, supporting cellular health and slowing ageing processes.

items.title: Immune system support
items.content: Vitamin C in the juice contributes to a stronger immune response and increased resistance to infections.

items.title: Anti‑inflammatory properties
items.content: Flavonoids and anthocyanins exhibit anti‑inflammatory effects, which may benefit chronic inflammatory conditions.

items.title: Cardiovascular health
items.content: Polysaccharides and potassium help maintain normal blood pressure and improve vascular function.

items.title: Digestive aid
items.content: A small amount of fibre remaining after pressing supports a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Berry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to blackberries, manifested as itching, swelling or rash.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although the juice is 100% natural, the inherent sugars in the fruit can be considerable; people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The acidic nature of the juice may irritate the stomach lining in persons with gastritis or ulcer disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink the juice chilled as a refreshing beverage, add it to smoothies, cocktails, meat sauces or desserts. It pairs well with mint, lemon and ginger.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the juice in the refrigerator at 0 °C‑4 °C in its original container. Once opened, consume within 5‑7 days. When frozen, the juice retains its qualities for up to 3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken Burrito Bowl is a Mexican‑inspired dish served in a bowl with rice, black beans, seasoned chicken pieces, fresh vegetables, guacamole and salsa. It combines the bold flavors of spices, lean protein, and wholesome carbs for a balanced, satisfying meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The bowl version emerged as a lighter alternative to the traditional wrapped burrito, offering the same ingredients without the tortilla.
Chicken is usually marinated in lime juice, chili, and cumin, giving it a distinctive aroma.
The Mexican rice used is often cooked with tomato paste and spices rather than plain boiled rice.
The dish is popular in fast‑casual chains across the US and Canada, often customizable with extra toppings.
Variations may replace chicken with beef, tofu, or seafood, but the classic chicken version remains the most common.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Rice and beans supply lasting energy and help maintain stable blood glucose levels.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: The bowl delivers vitamin C from salsa, vitamin K and potassium from avocado, and iron from beans.

items.title: Heart‑friendly fats
items.content: Monounsaturated fats in guacamole support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Beans and vegetables boost fiber content, aiding digestion.

items.title: Allergy to chicken or legumes
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken or beans.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared sauces and seasonings can be salty; people with hypertension should watch portions.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: The bowl can be calorie‑rich due to avocado and sauces; portion control is advisable.

items.title: Food safety concerns
items.content: Chicken must be fully cooked and beans properly boiled to avoid bacterial contamination.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the bowl in a large dish. You can stir all ingredients together or eat them separately, adding sauces to taste. For a lighter option, reduce guacamole and swap rice for quinoa.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared bowl in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat chicken and beans to at least 75 °C. Add avocado just before serving to prevent browning.

cereal-or-granola-bar-kelloggs-nutri-gra.title: Cereal or granola bar (Kellogg's Nutri-Grain Fruit and Nut Bar)

content.title: About
content.content: Kellogg's Nutri‑Grain Fruit and Nut Bar is a ready‑to‑eat snack bar that combines whole grains, dried fruit, nuts, and a modest amount of sugar. It is designed as a quick breakfast or on‑the‑go snack, providing energy and basic nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The bar blends whole‑grain cereal, dried apples, cranberries, and nuts.
It is sold in several flavor variations, including berry and nut‑fruit blends.
Each bar is individually wrapped for convenient portability.
Nutri‑Grain was first introduced in the 1990s as part of Kellogg's quick‑breakfast lineup.

items.title: Source of whole grains
items.content: Whole grains provide complex carbohydrates that release energy slowly and help maintain satiety.

items.title: Contains nuts and dried fruit
items.content: Nuts supply healthy monounsaturated fats, while dried fruit adds vitamins and antioxidants.

items.title: B‑vitamin enrichment
items.content: The bar is fortified with vitamins B1, B2 and B6, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestive health and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Convenient and portable
items.content: Ideal for a quick breakfast, a road‑trip snack, or post‑workout fuel.

items.title: Nut and gluten allergy
items.content: The product contains nuts and gluten‑bearing grains; individuals with these allergies should avoid it.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Added sugars are present, so people monitoring glucose intake should account for it.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: One bar provides roughly 200 kcal, so portion control is advisable for calorie‑restricted diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The bar is ready to eat straight from the package. It can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, chopped into yogurt, sliced into muesli, or used as an energy boost before exercise.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, consume within 7‑10 days for best quality.

content.title: About
content.content: Ghee is clarified butter obtained by slowly heating butter to evaporate water and separate milk proteins. The result is pure fat with a characteristic nutty aroma. Ghee is widely used in Indian and Middle Eastern cuisines.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ghee has a higher smoke point (around 250 °C) than regular butter, making it suitable for high‑heat cooking.
Traditionally ghee is made at home, but it is now readily available in health food stores.
In Indian culinary tradition ghee is considered a "five‑element" food that balances flavors and energy.
Ghee can be stored at room temperature for several months without spoiling because the milk solids are removed.

items.title: Rich in healthy fats
items.content: Ghee contains saturated and monounsaturated fatty acids that can provide sustained energy and promote satiety.

items.title: Source of vitamins A and D
items.content: The clarification process concentrates fat‑soluble vitamins that support vision, immunity, and bone health.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Ghee provides butyric acid, which may benefit gut lining and digestive function.

items.title: Lactose‑ and casein‑free
items.content: Almost all lactose and milk proteins are removed during clarification, making ghee suitable for those with lactose intolerance or casein allergy.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) present in ghee has antioxidant effects.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Ghee is a concentrated source of energy, so it should be used in moderation.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: A large proportion of the fat is saturated; people with high cholesterol should limit intake.

items.title: Milk‑protein allergy
items.content: Although most proteins are removed, individuals with severe milk allergies may still react.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use ghee for sautéing, frying, and baking, add it to sauces, porridges, soups, and baked goods. A small spoonful in tea or coffee gives a creamy, nutty flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store ghee in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct light. At room temperature it stays fresh for several months, and in the refrigerator it can last up to a year.

content.title: About
content.content: Grits are a corn‑based cereal available in regular and quick varieties. Cooking them with water creates a low‑calorie dish without added fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Grits are a staple in the Southern United States, especially in South Carolina and Georgia.
Pure corn grits are gluten‑free, provided no wheat additives are used.
Quick‑cook grits are ready in 5‑7 minutes, while regular grits take about 20‑25 minutes.
They are often served with cheese, butter, or seafood, but can also be sweet with honey and berries.
The yellow hue comes from carotenoids naturally present in corn.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: When prepared with water, grits contain virtually no fat, making them suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Corn grits provide slow‑releasing energy, helping maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Grits provide thiamine (B1), niacin (B3) and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: They contain magnesium, phosphorus and iron, which are essential for bones and blood formation.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn products.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Grits have a relatively high GI, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Aflatoxin risk
items.content: Poor‑quality corn can contain aflatoxins; choose products from reputable suppliers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bring water to a boil, add the grits and simmer until the desired consistency is reached. Serve sweet with honey, berries and nuts, or savory with cheese, herbs, vegetables, or seafood.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store grits in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For long‑term storage, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent mold growth.

content.title: About
content.content: Turkey is the meat of the domestic turkey (Meleagris gallopavo), a bird native to North America. The breast is white, lean, and tender meat, while the thigh and drumstick are dark, juicier, and fattier. Turkey is roasted, stewed, fried, and grilled, and ground turkey is made into patties and sausages.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkeys are native to North America and were domesticated more than a thousand years ago.
In the United States, roast turkey is the main dish of Thanksgiving.
Turkey breast is leaner than the thigh and drumstick.
The common belief that turkey makes you sleepy because of tryptophan is exaggerated: it has about as much as other meats.
Turkey is made into fillets, ground meat, sausages, and cold cuts.

items.title: Source of complete protein
items.content: Turkey provides protein with all the essential amino acids.

items.title: Contains B vitamins
items.content: It contains niacin, B6, and B12, which help produce energy and form blood cells.

items.title: Contains selenium
items.content: Selenium is an antioxidant trace mineral that is important for the thyroid.

items.title: Contains zinc and phosphorus
items.content: These minerals support immunity and bone health.

items.title: Breast is lean
items.content: Skinless breast is low in fat and high in protein.

items.title: Undercooked meat
items.content: Undercooked turkey may contain Salmonella and Campylobacter; the meat should be cooked to 74 °C (165 °F) inside.

items.title: Cross-contamination
items.content: Raw meat and its juices should not come into contact with cooked food, cutting boards, and dishes without washing.

items.title: Skin and fat
items.content: The skin and dark meat contain more fat and calories.

items.title: Processed products
items.content: Turkey sausages, ham, and cold cuts contain a lot of salt and additives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Turkey is roasted whole or in parts, stewed, fried, grilled, added to soups, and ground turkey is made into patties. The breast dries out easily, so do not overcook it; it can be marinated or roasted in a bag. For safety, the meat must reach 74 °C (165 °F) inside.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store raw turkey in the refrigerator in a covered container for no more than one to two days, or freeze it. Thaw meat in the refrigerator. Keep cooked meat in the refrigerator for up to three to four days. Do not leave meat at room temperature for more than two hours.
